summary: Defines an experimental scheme for Internet encapsulation, in which IP datagrams get an extra header and are routed between encapsulators and decapsulators along flows. The authors were Woodburn and Mills. It is an Experimental protocol, version 1.

plainLanguage.summary: It puts a letter inside a bigger envelope for a part of the trip, and a helper at the other end removes the extra envelope.

questions: what is the internet encapsulation protocol
what is a flow id in encapsulation
subtitle: A scheme for tunneling datagrams through intermediate networks.

tldr.problem: Networks need a way to tunnel datagrams through intermediate networks to bypass routing failures, avoid broken gateways, or establish deterministic paths for experimentation.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol wraps an original datagram in an Encapsulation Header and sends it to a Decapsulator, which removes the wrapper and forwards the original datagram. Encapsulators and Decapsulators form virtual networks through configured flows.
tldr.outcome: This version 1 specification provides an experimental standard for IP-based encapsulation that does not require source routing or IP options, making it more flexible for tunneling multiple protocols.

today: RFC 1241 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted. It provided an early approach to encapsulation and tunneling before more widely adopted mechanisms like GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) were developed.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 1241 defines an experimental protocol for encapsulating IP datagrams. Tunneling is the practice of sending one datagram through intermediate networks using a path that circumvents conventional routing mechanisms. Traditional tunneling used IP source routing options, which require the source to know about network topology and have limited router support. This RFC proposes a cleaner solution: a new encapsulation protocol that wraps the original datagram in a new IP header and protocol header, then routes the wrapped datagram through an encapsulation space between special entities called Encapsulators and Decapsulators.

The key benefit is transparency: the source application does not need to know encapsulation is occurring, and the destination receives the original datagram intact. Virtual networks can be created by linking otherwise unconnected machines through configured flows in the encapsulation space.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking every router on the path, you just wrap up your package and address it to a special helper. The helper knows the whole route.

sections.title: Architecture and Flows
sections.content:
An Encapsulator is a host or gateway that receives a Clear Datagram (the original IP datagram) from a user space and decides whether encapsulation should be used. When encapsulation is needed, the Encapsulator performs a mapping function that matches the datagram's headers against stored patterns to determine a Flow ID. This Flow ID acts as a key into a table containing information about where the datagram should go.

The Encapsulator then prepends an Encapsulation Header (which itself contains an IP header) to the Clear Datagram, creating an Encapsulated Datagram. This is then forwarded to a Decapsulator whose address was looked up in the flow information table. The Decapsulator removes the encapsulation header and treats the Clear Datagram as if it were received locally. If the datagram has not reached its final destination, the Decapsulator may become an Encapsulator and encapsulate the datagram again for the next leg of its journey.
sections.plainLanguage: The Encapsulator wraps the package and ships it to a Decapsulator. If the Decapsulator is not the final destination, it becomes an Encapsulator and wraps it again.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Header
sections.content:
The Encapsulation Header consists of two parts: an outer IP header and an Encapsulation Protocol Header. The outer IP header is constructed by mapping fields from the Clear Header (the original IP header) according to specific rules. Most fields in the Clear Header are simply ignored. Quality of Service (QoS) bits and Precedence are copied to preserve the requested service level. The More Fragments and Fragment Offset bits are not copied because the Encapsulated Datagram is a complete new datagram regardless of the original's fragmentation state.

The Encapsulation Protocol Header contains a 4-bit version field (version 1), a 4-bit header length field, a 4-bit message type field (value 1 for data messages, 2 for error messages), a 4-bit reason code field, a 16-bit one's complement checksum, and a 32-bit Flow ID. The Flow ID is local to the Encapsulator; different Encapsulators along the same flow may use different Flow ID values.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapper has a return address (the Encapsulator), a destination (the Decapsulator), and a label (the Flow ID) saying what kind of package it is.

sections.title: Mapping Functions and Flow Tables
sections.content:
To decide which flow a datagram belongs to, the Encapsulator uses a mask-and-match table lookup. The Clear Header is matched against stored headers and masks to determine the Flow ID. The masks allow a range of source and destination addresses to map to a single flow. Other fields such as IP Type of Service bits or even TCP port numbers can be used to discriminate between flows. This flexibility allows very fine-grained control: a given network can be associated with a particular flow, or even a particular TCP connection.

Once the Flow ID is determined, the Encapsulator looks up information about the flow in an Encapsulation Info table. This table entry contains the Decapsulator's address in the Encapsulation Space, the Flow ID as seen by the Decapsulator, and if this is not the first Encapsulator along the flow, the previous Encapsulator's address and its local Flow ID for error reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Tables at the Encapsulator say: packages like this go to this Decapsulator with this label.

sections.title: Decapsulation and Error Handling
sections.content:
A Decapsulator receiving an Encapsulated Datagram has the option to bypass the expensive mask-and-match operation by using the received Flow ID to point directly to its local tables for constructing the next Encapsulation Header. If the Flow ID is unknown, the Decapsulator sends an error message back to the previous Encapsulator. Because the Decapsulator is bypassing the normal IP forwarding mechanism when using Flow IDs, it must manually decrement the Time To Live (TTL) field before re-encapsulation occurs. If the TTL expires, the Decapsulator sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message to the source in the Clear Header.

Two types of error messages are defined: one to report unknown Flow IDs, and another to forward ICMP error messages backward along the flow to the original source Encapsulator. When an ICMP message is received by an Encapsulator regarding a flow, it forwards the message backward along the flow by translating the Flow ID in the message to the Flow ID relative to the previous Encapsulator.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong in the Encapsulation Space, messages go back to say the package was lost or couldn't be delivered.
